sections.COMMENTS:
This Individual Source is part of the system of blind faults confined at the footwall of the Acquasanta thrust activated during the 2009 Lâ€™Aquila seismic sequence, further activated during  January 2017 by the 2016-2017 central Italy sequence (Bigi et al., 2013; Tondi et al., 2020; Buttinelli et al., 2021).
The 2009 L'Aquila sequence, besides hitting the town of L'Aquila, struck a portion of the Central Apennines that was believed to be especially well known from a seismotectonic point of view. The projection of the northern reaches of the 2009 sequence onto geological cross-sections shows that the 9 April 2009 event unfolded on a fault segment belonging to a deeper thrust sheet independent from the shallower Gorzano fault (Bigi et al., 2013).
The region is undergoing SW-NE active extension and is affected by strong earthquakes with magnitude up to 7.0. The normal faulting focal mechanisms computed for the largest shocks agree with the tectonic regime of the region (Pondrelli et al., 2010; Scognamiglio et al., 2010; Herrmann et al., 2011).
This SW-dipping Individual Source is part of a fault system formed during the Mesozoic and reactivated during the Miocene flexure of the foreland in response to the orogenic build-up (e.g., Tondi et al., 2020). Some of the faults formed in the previous tectonic regime were transported onto the Acquasanta thrust hanging-wall (i.e., the Monti della Laga - Gorzano fault, MLG), whereas their roots remained confined at the thrust footwall.
The interpretation of seismic reflection profiles in the area (Di Bucci et al., 2021; www.retrace3d.it) allowed to image the geometry of the whole Acquasanta thrust (Buttinelli et al., 2021), dipping toward W-NW. This evidence has shown that the southern segment of the MLG in the Campotosto Lake area is detached at shallow levels, thus indicating that seismicity like that due to the 9 April 2009 (Mw 5.4) earthquake has occurred below the Acquasanta thrust (Bigi et al., 2013; Buttinelli et al., 2021).

pictures.t: Map of the 2009 seismic sequence and active faults
pictures.c: Map and cross-sections showing the 2009 earthquake seismic sequence and the Quaternary surface faults (from EMERGEO Working Group [2009]).
Historical and instrumental earthquakes (a), and geological sketch (b) of the central Apennines (from Vannoli et al. [2012]).

pictures.t: Seismotectonic sketch of the central Apennines
pictures.c: Synoptic view of the active faults and the seismogenic sources (DISS, version 3.1.1) of the central Apennines. Notice that the main extensional sources terminate to the northwest and to the southeast at the transverse OASL and ORL, respectively (from Vannoli et al. [2012]).

pictures.t: Map of the 2009 earthquake coseismic ground deformation by EmerGeo Working Group (2009)
pictures.c: Map of the field observations of coseismic ground ruptures (from EMERGEO Working Group [2009]). Note that tectonic ruptures were identified along the Paganica Fault, where they were interpreted as due to primary surface faulting, and along a set of synthetic and antithetic faults bordering the L'Aquila Basin.
Map showing the 2009 earthquake epicentral area in the seismotectonic framework of the Central Apennines (from Falcucci et al. [2009]).

pictures.t: Map and cross-sections of relocated earthquakes of the 2009 sequence
pictures.c: Relocated events of the 2009 earthquake sequence, the cross-sections show the geometry at depth of the seismogenic source (pannel b) and its position respect to nearby sources (panel c) (from Chiarabba et al. [2009]). Note the cutoff of the seismicity at 2-3 km of depth (Sez-2, panel b) and its projection towards the Paganica Fault surface trace.

pictures.t: Map of the relocated 2009 earthquake sequence
pictures.c: Map of relocated events of the 2009 earthquake sequence and traces of Quaternary normal faults (from Chiarabba et al. [2009]). The Mw 5.4, 9 April 2009 aftershock and the related sequence activated a structure located to the NNE, with a right en-echelon step respect to the Mw 6.3 earthquake seismogenic source.

pictures.t: Map of RCMT solutions of the 2009 earthquake sequence
pictures.c: Focal mechanisms of the 2009 seismic sequence constraining seismogenic source geometry and T and P axes orientation (from Pondrelli et al., [2010]).

pictures.t: Source model and slip distribution of the 6 April 2009 main shock (from Walters et al. [2009])
pictures.c: Fault model and variable slip distribution of the seismogenic source of the 6 April 2009 earthquake from inversion of SAR and GPS data (from Walters et al. [2009]). Note that the modeled fault is longer than the outcrop exposure of the Paganica Fault and is in overlap with the Monte Stabiata Fault.

pictures.t: Geological data in Mt. Gorzano area
pictures.c: Geological and seismological data. The projection of the 2009 earthquake sequence onto the geological cross-sections shows that the 2009 sequence developed in a deeper thrust sheet on a fault plane independent from the Gorzano fault (Bigi et al., [2013])

pictures.t: Ground deformation induced by the 18 January 2017 earthquakes
pictures.c: Modeled and observed DInSAR data (panels a, c, and d), GPS data (panel e), and fault dislocation model (panel b) of the 18 January 2017 events. Highest slip values are located in an about 5 Ã— 5 km2 region, spanning 3- to 9-km depth, with a peak slip of about 0.58 m (Falcucci et al., [2018])
